Where it began

Robert Key was born in East Dulwich, London, on 12 May 1979, and grew up in a family that loved its sport. At Worsley Bridge Primary he helped the school win cricket cups for both Bromley and Kent, which put him into the county under-elevens. Kent's youth coach Alan Ealham took him under his wing, and he was also good enough at tennis to play it for the county.

He was in Kent's second eleven at 16. In 1997 he helped England's under-17s win a youth tournament in Bermuda, and in 1998 he opened the batting for the England side that won the 1998 Under-19 World Cup in South Africa.

The player

He made his first-class debut for Kent in 1998 and a hundred against Durham in his first season. A spell at the National Academy followed, and in 2002 he won his first Test cap, against India. He went on to play 15 Tests from 2002 to 2005, making 775 runs at 31.00 with one hundred and three fifties.

That one hundred was a big one. Recalled against the West Indies at Lord's in 2004, he drove and pulled his way to 221, sharing a stand of 291 with Andrew Strauss, then a second-wicket record for the ground. He even met the Queen at tea on the first day and carried on regardless. Later in the series his unbeaten 93 at Old Trafford took England home, chasing a record fourth-innings total for a winning side there. Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year.

What made him special

He was a strong, positive batsman who drove and pulled with real power, and at his best he simply piled up runs. In 2004 he reached a thousand for the season on 2 June and at one stage made five hundreds in seven innings. His career-best, 270 not out, came for Kent in 2009.

He could bat all day when set: in 2005 he and Martin van Jaarsveld put on 323 against Surrey, then a Kent record for the third wicket, in a match where he made two hundreds.

Away from the middle

Kent made him captain when David Fulton stood down. He led them to the Twenty20 Cup in 2007 and the second division title in 2010, and after one season off he took the job back until 2015. He retired in April 2016.

By then he was already a familiar voice on television, and once he stopped playing he was in demand as a commentator and pundit across several outlets. In April 2022 he gave all that up to become managing director of the England men's team, and one of his first moves was to bring in Brendon McCullum to coach the Test side.

And finally

He took his first first-class wicket at the start of the 2009 season, more than a decade after his debut. Patience, it seems, is a virtue for bowlers as well as openers.
